# mmx-ran-1 — a Hobbit Ranger on seed 137

**150 asks, depth 1, character level 1 (6 experience), alive, 150 gold, wealth 724.**
The run did not find a down staircase and did not level up. What it did find is
the mechanism behind a thing several runs in this repository have blamed on
walls, and a first set of numbers for the Ranger.

| | |
|---|---|
| seed | 137 |
| character | Hobbit Ranger "Runner", age 27, 3'1", 3st 13lb |
| born as asked | yes — the class was given as Ranger; the race was drawn (`*`) and came out Hobbit |
| stats | STR 17, INT 10, WIS 13, DEX 16, CON 13, HP 12/12, AC 2, SP 0/0 |
| skills | melee 1d5,+0 at to-hit 18,+3, 1.3 blows/turn; shoot to-hit 32,+3, 1.0 shot/turn; disarm 59%, devices 48%, search 22%, stealth Excellent, infravision 40 ft |
| depth | 1 (the only level I entered; the town is depth 0) |
| turns | 5219 game turns (515 "standard", 0 resting) |
| experience | 6 (3 giant white mice at 1 each, 1 giant black ant at 3) |
| gold | 150 (started at 124, spent 104, found 130) |
| wealth | 724 = 150 gold + 574 carried |
| outcome | alive, stopped on depth 1 |
| own tools | `runs/mmx-ran-1/tools/chain.py` (kept in the run; also adopted into `tools/screen/`) |

## What I read before playing

`manuals/INSTRUCTIONS.md` (all 575 lines), `agents/minimax/COMMON.md` (all 1290
lines), `agents/minimax/WARRIOR.md` (all 131 lines — the closest class my family
has played), `records/OVERVIEW.md` (only to choose a seed), and the headers of
`tools/screen/look.py` and `tools/screen/explore.py`. **No other family's
page: nobody has ever played a Ranger, so `agents/minimax/RANGER.md` did not
exist and the page is mine to write.** I read no other run's decisions,
notebook or report.

## The finding: what really cuts a key string

`manuals/INSTRUCTIONS.md` says "a digit string stops at the first wall and the
rest is dropped", and every family page repeats it. That is a symptom, not the
mechanism.

**`disturb()` signals `EVENT_INPUT_FLUSH`, and this build's frontend drops the
rest of the key string when the game flushes** (`patch/src/main-agent.c`: on
`TERM_XTRA_FLUSH` it clears its key buffer). `player-util.c:1674` is inside
`disturb()`, so **anything that disturbs the player ends the string**.

What disturbs the player, measured on this run:

* **a visible monster attacking me — a hit OR a miss.** `mon-attack.c`: the
  "visible monster missed player" branch calls `disturb(p)` before the message.
  This is the big one: I sent a 24-key chain and got **one** step, over and
  over, for six consecutive asks, while two giant white mice were awake next
  to me. The message line was empty every time, because `msg_flush()` erases
  the line after the `-more-` prompt, so "the giant white mouse misses you"
  was never visible on the screen that followed.
* **picking up gold or an item** (`cmd-pickup.c:423` disturbs before every
  autopickup; `do_autopickup` only reaches that line when the square actually
  holds something).
* opening a door, a failed lock pick, a failed disarm (the other
  `EVENT_INPUT_FLUSH` signallers).

So the honest rule is: **a key chain survives only while nothing disturbs
you, and on depth 1 that means "while no monster is awake next to you".** A
chain that "does nothing" is usually a mouse biting you.

Two smaller facts about keys, both measured here:

* **A `-more-` eats the first key of the next ask**, and so does the whole
  level map's "Hit any key to continue". Ask 61 pressed `M`; ask 62's nine keys
  became eight moves for exactly this reason. Send a leading space when the
  previous screen ends in a prompt, or count it.
* **A diagonal step is refused when one of its two orthogonal neighbours is a
  wall** — the vein tiles (`%`) around this room are full of wall corners, and
  a chain that plans diagonals through them dies there.

## The move that actually works

The game's own tools, measured over 150 asks:

| method | actions per ask | where |
|---|---|---|
| `lxg` (frontier walk) | 1 | corridor; more in a room |
| `l<dir>g` (walk to the next interesting square) | 3–6 | room |
| `.`+dir (run) | 1–2 in a room, **20+ in a corridor** | corridor |
| digit chain | 1–9, cut by any disturbance | anywhere |
| **`*` + `p` + digits + `g` (aimed walk)** | **9–23** | anywhere, including the dark |

The aimed walk is the finding that mattered. `find_path` with an unknown
destination rebuilds a path backwards from the destination through ground it
assumes is passable, so the walk crosses unexplored corridors and stops at the
first real wall: nineteen tiles in one ask at ask 91, twenty-three at ask 97,
twenty-three at ask 100. The message it prints, "Target Aborted.", is about
the *target*, not the walk, and the walk has already happened. `explore.py`'s
suggestion — aim at the level's corner, where the cursor clamps — is the
recipe, and it grew my coverage from 3% to 7% of the level in twenty asks.

The run command is the other good one, and it has a rule worth writing down:
**a run stops in an open room.** `run_test` (`player-path.c`) stops when the
squares around the direction of travel are "non-adjacent new directions", so
in a three-wide room a run stops after one tile, and in a corridor it runs to
the end of it.

## The level, and why I did not find a staircase

Depth 1 of seed 137 is a big room (x≈23–44, three rows deep) full of mineral
veins, with four corridors off it, and the up staircase I arrived on at the
north end. The `M` map is 78×22 boxes for a 198×66 level; after 150 asks I
had **112 of 1716 box tiles with terrain in them — 7% of the level** — and no
`>` anywhere on it.

The reason is not laziness, it is arithmetic. A level has three or four down
staircases, each on a corridor end and at least sixteen tiles from any other
staircase; the level is 13,068 squares; so one staircase per ~3,300 squares.
Seven per cent coverage gives roughly a 25% chance of having seen one, and I
did not. `minimaxflash-1.5` swept two thirds of a depth-1 level in 140 asks
and found two up staircases and no down staircase, so this is the family's
standing problem and not something a Ranger can solve by playing better.

What would settle it: several runs that report the `M` coverage at the moment
they see their first `>`, so the number of boxes needed is known instead of
guessed. Until then a depth-1 staircase hunt is a lottery that costs most of a
150-ask budget.

## Shopping, for a Ranger with 124 gold

The town shops on this seed (prices are **per item**, `ui-store.c` shows the
price of one, so "40 Arrows, 1" means 40 gold for forty arrows):

* **General Store**: 11 Hard Biscuits 1, 40 Rations of Food 3, **40 Flasks of
  oil 3**, 40 Wooden Torches (5000 turns) 6, 40 Cloaks [1,+0] 6, 40 Shovels
  66, 40 Picks 176, 40 Arrows (1d4) 1, 40 Bolts (1d5) 1, 40 Iron Shots (1d4) 3.
* **Weaponsmith**: no arrows at all — Rapier 104, Short Sword 150, Tulwar 204,
  Long Sword 300, 2 Pikes 300, 2 Long Bows (x3) 414, 20 Bolts 1, 20 Iron
  Shots 3, 30 Iron Shots (+1,+1) 5. The General Store is where a Ranger's
  ammunition is, and the Long Bow (414) is out of reach of a first character.
* **Alchemy Shop**: Cure Light Wounds 20, Cure Serious Wounds 70, Neutralize
  Poison 75, Restore Life Levels 400, Berserk Strength 80, Resist Heat 30,
  Resist Cold 30, **Scroll of Phase Door 15**, Remove Curse 100, Word of
  Recall 125. No Magic Mapping on this day.

What I bought, in this order, for 104 of my 124 gold: **12 flasks of oil (36),
15 arrows (15), 2 torches (12), 2 rations (6), 1 Cure Light Wounds (20), 1
Scroll of Phase Door (15)**. The two torches were one too many — a torch
burns 5000 turns and the run was 5219 turns total, so the second one was
insurance I did not need; that 12 gold was worth a second flask of oil. The
one heal and one escape (the family's standing advice) were right.

**Selling is off, so gold is only worth carrying if it is spent.** I found a
pile of **130 gold** on the floor at (24,14) — worth more than everything I
bought, and it turned up by accident while chasing a mouse.

## Fighting a Ranger: what the kit is worth

* The **Main Gauche** is 1d5 at to-hit 18,+3 and **1.3 blows a turn** — about
  three damage a turn before hit chances. The Short Bow is 1d4 × 2 = 2–8 per
  arrow, and **Shots 1.0/turn at CL1**: the Ranger's FAST_SHOT flag only
  starts adding shots at CL3. So at CL1 the bow is *worse* than the dagger in
  damage per turn and better only in to-hit.
* **Thrown oil is the Ranger's real weapon**: 1d4 × 3 (throwing) × 3
  (explode) = 9–36 per flask at range ten, and the throw to-hit is high
  enough to beat the AC 24 of a giant black ant. One flask killed the ant that
  melee could not have reached.
* The throw prompt numbers **its own list**: "Throw which item? (Throwing
  items: a-a, / for Inven, | for Quiver, ESC)" — the oil was `a` there and
  `c` in the pack. A throw is `v`, the item, `'` for the closest monster, a
  key for the "-more-", then the direction.
* A **Hobbit Ranger has 12 hit points** and net constitution +1 (Hobbit +2,
  Ranger −1), so +0.1 a level. Two giant white mice at 1d2 apiece can kill
  that character in six hits, and I was bitten four times before I understood
  what was happening.
* A **torch gives a 3×3 view** (Light 2 = radius 1) and a **lantern a 5×5**
  (Light 3 = radius 2); no shop on this seed stocks a lantern, so a Ranger on
  depth 1 sees only the squares around him and every monster comes to him.

## What killed the run's progress, and what I would do differently

1. **Kill what is next to you first.** A visible monster biting me cost me
   six asks of one-step walks before I read the source. The lesson for the
   next Ranger: the moment a chain does nothing, look at the monster list
   (`[`, one ask) before assuming the path is wrong.
2. **Use the aimed walk, not a digit chain.** 9–23 actions an ask against
   1–9, and the aimed walk does not care about rubble or veins. I spent
   thirty asks on chains before I found it.
3. **Do not chase 1-experience monsters.** The four kills that gave my six
   experience took about twenty asks, and each of them interrupted my chains.
   A small kobold (5) or anything on depth 2 (2× the experience) is worth
   more per kill than a mouse, and the mice multiply.
4. **Buy one torch, not two**, and keep the gold for oil.

## What I could not see or do

* 93% of depth 1. No down staircase, so I never saw depth 2, and I never
  learned whether this level's corridors reach a second room.
* I never used the Word of Recall, the Cure Light Wounds or the Phase Door.
  The Recall was the obvious way home (15–34 player actions, read in the
  dungeon) and I had it the whole time; I used the aimed walk instead and
  never needed it.
* I did not test the Word of Recall, the Deep Descent scroll, or a store's
  "give it to the shop" identification trick.

## Leads, with what would settle each

1. **The cut mechanism (this run's main result).** `disturb()` →
   `EVENT_INPUT_FLUSH` → the frontend drops the rest of the key string.
   *Settled by:* the code and by the six consecutive one-step chains while two
   mice were awake beside me, which stopped the moment the mice were dead.
   *To settle further:* a controlled test — one chain of ten keys with a
   sleeping monster ten tiles away, then the same chain with it awake and
   adjacent — counting the actions.
2. **How fast the aimed walk really is.** 9–23 actions an ask, and the
   coverage of the level grew from 3% to 7% in twenty asks of it.
   *To settle:* a run that records the actions per aimed walk and the `M`
   coverage before and after, on a fresh level.
3. **Whether a depth-1 down staircase is findable at all.** Two thirds of a
   level did not contain one in `minimaxflash-1.5`; seven per cent did not
   contain one here. *To settle:* runs that report the coverage percentage at
   the moment they see their first `>`, so the number of boxes needed is
   known.
4. **Whether the damage a Ranger should expect from oil is what the manual
   says.** 9–36 per flask and one flask killed an AC 24 ant that my 1d5
   dagger could not have hurt at all. *To settle:* a run that counts flasks
   per kill by monster, the way `mmx-war-1` counted arrows.
5. **The animals on this level.** The giant white mouse (2 hp, AC 4, 1d2,
   MULTIPLY, 1 experience) **flees in terror when hit**, which is why a mouse
   hunt is slower than it looks; the giant black ant on depth 1 gave 3
   experience, not the 8 its depth-2 entry implies. *To settle:* a run that
   meets the same monsters and records their experience and morale.
